title: AI Slump Revives Asia's Forgotten Trades as Investors Turn to China and India
excerpt: Bloomberg reports a broadening rotation out of crowded AI supply-chain stocks: the Nifty 50 just had its best week since 2021 on $1.9 billion of foreign buying, and a Hong Kong gauge of mainland shares its best week since March 2025.
body:
• The unwinding AI trade after the US midterms is pushing global investors toward out-of-favour Chinese and Indian stocks and toward healthcare, consumer and domestically driven Asian companies, Bloomberg reports.
  • India's Nifty 50 gained 8.6 percent last week, its best week since 2021, as foreign funds poured a net $1.9 billion into local shares through Wednesday.
  • A Hong Kong gauge of mainland Chinese companies gained 5.2 percent last week, its best performance since March 2025.
  • Not everyone is leaving AI: some investors see the selloff as a buying opportunity, and foreigners are still expected to keep selling Asia's AI supply-chain stocks for now.

The unraveling of the AI trade after the US midterm elections is forcing investors to rethink their Asia playbook, reviving demand for out-of-favour Chinese and Indian stocks and for companies set to benefit from easing inflation and trade tensions, Bloomberg reports.

Asia has been among the hardest hit by the fallout from the Democrats' sweep of Congress. Many of the region's biggest stocks — Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing among them — are critical suppliers to the global AI build-out, which leaves local markets exposed as investors brace for greater scrutiny of the industry and question whether massive spending on computing infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.

"I expect investors to diversify more broadly and reduce their concentration in the AI trade. This should be supportive of China and other markets where valuations are less demanding."

— Rajeev De Mello, global macro portfolio manager, Gama Asset Management

China and India as hedges

Aberdeen Investments favours markets powered by stronger domestic growth, including India and Vietnam, and sees upside in Chinese technology firms. Hao Hong, chief investment officer at Lotus Asset Management, said he is betting against oil and petrochemical firms and going long precious metals and Hong Kong equity futures. A Hong Kong gauge tracking mainland companies gained 5.2 percent last week, its best performance since March 2025. Jason Lui, head of Asia-Pacific equity and derivatives strategy at BNP Paribas, said some global investors are looking at China's onshore market as a diversifier for AI-heavy portfolios.

India's appeal has grown as oil prices declined on expectations of an earlier end to the Iran war, easing a key pressure point for the energy-importing economy, and the market's lack of AI exposure is now seen as an advantage. LOGOS Asset Management's Charlie Hong said he sold his SK Hynix, Samsung, Intel and Lumentum shares last month and has since boosted Indian holdings in new-age technology companies, financial firms and contract drug manufacturers. The Nifty 50 gained 8.6 percent last week, its best week since 2021, and foreign funds poured a net $1.9 billion into local shares through Wednesday. Before these gains, benchmarks in India and China had ranked among the world's worst-performing indexes this year through October.

Beyond AI, beyond two markets

The rotation is reaching overlooked corners of Asia as well. Allianz Global Investors sees healthcare and consumer staples benefiting while defence and financial stocks could underperform. In Korea, Fidelity's Dale Nicholls sees early signs of rotation beyond the semiconductor heavyweights among domestic pension funds, pointing to consumption-related areas from wellness to K-pop agencies and beauty companies — stocks ACG Management's Hui Ling Loh also favours because they are domestically oriented and face limited US tariff and policy risk. Rayliant's Phillip Wool holds LG Electronics, whose US sales of televisions, refrigerators and washing machines could gain if tariff pressure eases, and the prospect of less isolationist US trade policy has lifted confidence in automakers including Toyota and Hyundai.

What to watch

Two cautions run through the reporting. India could benefit from the rotation, De Mello said, although its dependence on imported energy remains a headwind. And not everyone is ready to abandon AI: some investors say the selloff may offer a chance to buy the dip given the sector's longer-term growth prospects. For now, though, the prevalent mood is caution — Emmer Capital's Manishi Raychaudhuri expects foreigners to keep selling Asia's AI "picks and shovels" stocks, and notes that India and China are the only two large, liquid markets offering a considerable array of non-AI exposures.
